TUI.NET

Testing

The Tuinet.Testing namespace ships in the library: an in-memory tty, a driver for whole apps, styled snapshots and screen assertions.

Rendering into a buffer

UI code is just a function from state to cells, so you can test it without a terminal. Render into a CellBuffer and assert on its text and styles:

[Fact]
public void Shows_the_title()
{
    var buffer = new CellBuffer(80, 24);
    new ShowcaseApp().Render(buffer, nowMs: 0);
    Assert.Contains("ITEMS · 20", buffer.ToString());
    Assert.Equal(Color.Hex(0xF5A623), buffer[2, 4].Style.Fg);   // the list's amber border
}

Driving an app

To drive a whole app, Tuinet.Testing.TestTerminal runs an IApp the way Terminal.Run does: a real Terminal over the in-memory TestTty, a frame after each input, and a clock the test sets. Calls chain, and Click("Save") clicks wherever that text is on screen:

[Fact]
public void Enter_edits_the_selected_item()
{
    using var term = new TestTerminal(new ShowcaseApp(), 110, 34);
    term.Press("jj").Key(KeyCode.Enter);
    Assert.Contains("EDIT ITEM · 03", term.Text);
    term.Click("Close");
    Assert.DoesNotContain("EDIT ITEM", term.Text);
    Assert.Equal(Color.Hex(0xF5A623), term.Screen.StyleOf("ITEMS · 20").Fg);
}
TestTerminal Does
Press("jj"), Press('s', Modifiers.Ctrl), Key(KeyCode.Tab, Modifiers.Shift) Key presses, a frame after each (\n is Enter, \t Tab, \u001b Esc)
Click(x, y), Click("Save"), Wheel(x, y, notches), Mouse(kind, x, y, button) Mouse reports
Paste(text), Resize(w, h), Post(message) Paste, resize and message events
Input("\u001b[1;5C") Raw bytes through the terminal's input parser
NowMs, Advance(ms) The clock; Advance sends a tick only when Run would wake (animating, or NextDueMs due)
Screen, Text, IsRunning, Terminal, Tty The last frame (a copy), its text, whether Handle returned false, and frame and byte counters

Assertions and snapshots

On a CellBuffer (using Tuinet.Testing;): FindText("Save") returns the cells the text covers (and shows the screen when it isn't there), StyleAt(x, y) and StyleOf("Save") read styles, ToAnsi() prints a frame in color in your terminal, and ToStyledString() writes it as markup, one line per row:

[fg=#E2E8F0 bg=#0D1117]  [fg=#F5A623]│[/]   [b]parse & validate intent[/]   [/]

Snapshot.Verify(buffer, "edit-form") compares that with __snapshots__/edit-form.txt next to the test file (styled: false compares the plain text). Trailing spaces and blank lines don't count. A missing or different snapshot fails the test and writes edit-form.received.txt beside it. To accept the new output, rename that file, or run TUINET_ACCEPT_SNAPSHOTS=1 dotnet test, then review the diff. Snapshot.Parse reads a snapshot back into a CellBuffer.

The snapshot folder is found from the test's source path. CI builds that map source paths (ContinuousIntegrationBuild, which turns /home/you/repo/tests/… into /_/tests/…) are handled by looking for the mapped folder above the test assembly; pass directory: to put snapshots elsewhere. Add *.received.txt to your .gitignore.

A snapshot is plain markup. When most of a row has one style with a background (a themed panel), that style opens the row and the tags inside it hold only what differs, so a dark theme doesn't repeat its background on every run. Hyperlinks and the cursor aren't part of the snapshot; assert those with buffer[x, y].Link and buffer.CursorX/CursorY.

The allocation guarantee is easy to test in your own app too: render into one CellBuffer in a loop and compare GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() before and after. Call the app directly for that, not through TestTerminal, which copies every frame.

Bytes on the wire

To test the bytes themselves, use a Terminal over a TestTty directly:

[Fact]
public void Key_in_frame_out()
{
    var tty = new TestTty(80, 24);
    using var term = new Terminal(tty);
    tty.Enqueue("j");

    Assert.True(term.Poll(out Event ev, 0));
    Assert.True(ev.Key.IsChar('j'));

    term.BeginFrame().SetString(0, 0, "moved");
    term.Present();
    Assert.Contains("moved", tty.WrittenText);
    Assert.Equal(1, tty.WriteCount);
}
